name: Liam Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Liam Ito, 58, and I help lay deck boards and fixings on a footbridge rebuild. I left school early and spent years in kitchens before coming to construction, so the senior carpenter still checks my first row. I like seeing people cross safely, but high platforms test my balance and every contract has an end.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture troubles me most because Mina’s desk work and my site wage could both be squeezed before robots reach the boards in 2031. Written staffing dates, paid tool practice and nearby vacancies would help us choose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to two earners when one is in an office and one is on a bridge. The dates hit our pay slips at different times.

headlineQuote: The dates hit our pay slips at different times.
portrait: Liam is a **58-year-old junior** footbridge worker who entered construction after years in restaurant kitchens.
He uses AI **occasionally** for fixing codes and adopts tools after they prove useful on site.
His **three-month buffer** faces risk from both his site work and Mina’s bus dispatch planning.
He seeks **paid local shifts** and tests new equipment before trusting claims about future work.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could squeeze Mina’s desk wage before robots threaten Liam’s physical work around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written staffing dates**, paid tool practice and real local vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew rebuilding the footbridge that a program can sort a delivery list, but we still have to line up the deck boards. I sometimes ask an AI tool what a fixing code means, then check the packet before using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a plateau would give me time to get better at setting the boards without a new system in the way. My partner Mina and I have about three months of expenses saved, but a long gap after the bridge contract would still hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would carry on taking paid footbridge shifts and ask the experienced carpenter to check my first row before I fasten the rest. In the first year I would check the contractor’s board for its next local job every Friday and keep our savings for a real gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel fairly settled at the bridge and a little uneasy about the next contract. The work is ordinary. The next site is never printed on my pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you end up on a bridge crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I left school early and spent years in restaurant kitchens before learning site work from a neighbour. I am 58 and still junior here, though I like seeing a deck people can actually walk across.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the first row hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the first row drifts, every later board follows it and the edge looks crooked. A senior carpenter catches it quickly; I am learning to see it before the screws go in.

say: I would say **delivery lists** can change, but people still line up deck boards.
I would check **fixing codes** against the packet before using anything.
think: A **slower pace** gives me room to improve on the footbridge.
Our **three-month reserve** cannot carry a long gap after this contract.
do: Keep taking **paid bridge shifts** and check the first row with a carpenter.
Check the **next-job board** every Friday during the first year.
feel: **Settled** on the current site, uneasy about the next job.
S0.quote: The next site is never printed on my pay slip.
fieldNote: Liam uses AI **occasionally** for fixing codes but relies on packaging and an experienced carpenter for actual work.
His **three-month cushion** supports a short gap; the bridge contract still has an end date.

steps.text: Keep taking paid footbridge deck shifts
Check the contractor next-job board every Friday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the foreman that faster plans might stop us waiting for materials, provided somebody checks the order before the lorry leaves. I would ask to see two accurate deliveries before the crew changes its routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If office scheduling becomes cheap, the contractor may book fewer days for the same bridge. I am slower at setting corners than the senior hands, so a compressed timetable could mean I am left off the next crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch the stores worker use the AI ordering checker on the next two loads, then try it if both loads arrive right. During the first year I would keep taking paid deck shifts and apply to the local fencing contractor if my bridge hours were cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel interested, then nervous when I think about how the new timetable gets decided. A good order helps only if there is still a paid day to install it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a wrong load?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the brackets are too short for the deck thickness, we lose half a morning and sometimes get blamed for delay. I would write that down rather than let the checker call the order a success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the fencing contractor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fencing firm posts vacancies from time to time and is on the same bus route. It is still physical work and robots could reach it later, but it could pay me during this change.

say: I would say **faster plans** help only when deliveries are correct.
I would ask for **two accurate loads** before changing the crew routine.
think: I fear a **compressed timetable** could leave me off the next crew.
My **slower corners** are exposed if the contractor only counts finished boards.
do: Try the **AI order checker** after watching two accurate loads.
Keep taking **paid deck shifts** in the first year.
Apply to the **local fencing firm** if bridge hours are cut.
feel: **Interested** in better orders, nervous about tighter booking.
S1.quote: A good order helps only if there is still a paid day to install it.
fieldNote: Liam will adopt **AI ordering** after specific evidence on two real loads, rather than a demonstration alone.
The **fencing application** is conditional on lost hours and offers a local wage, not a robot-proof trade.

steps.text: Try the AI order checker after two accurate deliveries
Keep taking paid footbridge deck shifts
Apply to the local fencing contractor if bridge hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that the 2028 system can draw a bridge before breakfast, but hands still fit boards until roughly 2031. I would ask the foreman for written dates on any robot trial instead of rumours at the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 60 in 2028, the office may be smaller and may price fewer labour hours into each job. At 63 in 2031, capable robots could lay the boards too, and three months of savings would not cover a long wait for a different trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid bridge shifts and collect the foreman’s signed list of boards and repairs I completed. In 2029 I would apply for the open maintenance post at the sports centre while staying on site; if robots replace us around 2031, Mina and I would ask the employment office what support bridges the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel badly shaken, though I could still make an application tomorrow. I am willing to learn a tool, but two years is short for rebuilding a working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why apply to the sports centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre has a paid vacancy now and I could patch fences or doors there while human hands are still needed. I would not tell Mina that maintenance is safe after capable robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mina say about using savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Mina dispatches buses, and she would want us to keep the reserve for rent rather than spend it on a course chosen in panic. Her desk work could change when the thinking AI arrives, so we would check both wages.

say: I would say **thinking AI** draws bridges before robots fit boards.
I would ask for **written robot dates** rather than site rumours.
think: At **60**, cheaper planning could reduce paid labour hours.
At **63**, capable robots and Mina’s exposed desk work could strain both wages.
do: Keep **paid bridge shifts** and collect signed work records.
Apply for **sports centre maintenance** in 2029 while employed.
Ask the **employment office** about support if robots take site tasks.
feel: **Shaken**, but able to act before the next contract ends.
S2.quote: I am willing to learn a tool, but two years is short for rebuilding a working life.
fieldNote: Liam sees **2028 thinking AI** as a risk to both site budgets and Mina’s bus dispatch work.
The **sports centre application** seeks near-term wages; he explicitly rejects any claim that maintenance survives robots.

steps.text: Keep taking paid footbridge shifts through 2029
Apply for the sports centre maintenance vacancy in 2029
Ask the employment office about support if robots take site tasks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that five years gives the contractor time to show us a real machine and a real staffing plan. I would ask for a trial on the bridge before deciding whether to learn its controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, thinking AI could do the drawings and Mina’s dispatch planning, while I still fit physical parts. At 66 in 2034, capable robots could take my board work as well, and I cannot assume retirement money covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working site shifts and ask to watch an AI-assisted layout tool on a crooked deck before training on it. In 2032 I would take paid bridge or fencing shifts and apply for a school grounds vacancy; if the tool proves useful, I would ask the foreman to train me during paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel more in control than in the fast picture, although I would still watch Mina’s job closely. Five years gives us time to check what is real and what is only a sales pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could school grounds work last beyond 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No one can promise that when robots can do outdoor work too. I would apply for paid years if the vacancy appeared, not pretend the title was protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in Mina’s work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my partner Mina whether the bus company was reducing dispatcher shifts as its planning software improved. We would use actual hours on her pay slips, not a headline, before deciding what we could spend.

say: I would ask for a **real machine trial** and staffing plan.
I would judge a tool on a **crooked deck**, not a clean demonstration.
think: At **63**, planning AI could touch Mina’s dispatch work while I still fit boards.
At **66**, robots could take my site tasks before our retirement income is known.
do: Watch the **AI layout tool** on a crooked deck before paid training.
Apply for a **school grounds** vacancy if posted.
feel: **More in control**, while watching both household wages.
S3.quote: Five years gives us time to check what is real and what is only a sales pitch.
fieldNote: Liam’s willingness to use the **layout tool** depends on a real crooked-deck trial and paid instruction.
His household risk includes **Mina’s dispatch planning**, which full thinking AI could affect in 2031.

steps.text: Train on the AI-assisted layout tool during paid hours if its trial works
Keep taking paid bridge or fencing shifts in 2032
Apply for a school grounds vacancy if posted

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade should allow employers to tell older site workers the truth about future shifts. I would ask the contractor to publish yearly numbers for the crews it still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I may be choosing shorter deck jobs because my balance on high platforms is not improving. At 71 in 2039, robots could take the remaining board work, while AI may already have changed Mina’s dispatch wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking safe ground-level repair shifts and add a little to savings after full-pay months. In 2037 I would check our rent and food costs with Mina, apply for a paid tool-store post if one appears locally, and decide on shorter hours only if both wages cover bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel time to plan, not permission to stop working. A decade can pass while a household keeps paying rent every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the tool store?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the stock well enough to learn the counter, and there are a few local shops, but software could manage orders and robots could move boxes. I would apply for a wage, not a safe harbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children contribute to retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children have their own homes, so I would not put their income into our budget. I would ask for help only in a real emergency, after Mina and I had checked our own options.

say: I would ask for **yearly paid-crew figures** from the contractor.
I would say **older site workers** deserve a clear account of future shifts.
think: At **68**, high platforms may be too risky for me even before robots.
At **71**, robots could end board work while Mina’s dispatch wage has also changed.
do: Keep taking **ground-level repairs** and add to savings in full-pay months.
Review **rent and food** with Mina in 2037.
Apply for a **local tool-store** post if paid work appears.
feel: **Time to plan**, but no comfort about stopping wages.
S4.quote: A decade can pass while a household keeps paying rent every month.
fieldNote: Liam plans for **balance and platform risk** as well as the later robot date.
The **tool-store application** is conditional, with explicit exposure to AI ordering and robotic stock movement.

steps.text: Keep taking safe ground-level repair shifts in 2037
Add to savings after full-pay months
Apply for a local paid tool-store post if one appears
